title: Pneumonia: Community or Hospital Acquired Changes the Pathway
bottomLine: Pneumonia management starts with severity and acquisition context. Distinguish community-acquired disease from hospital/healthcare-associated risk patterns, identify aspiration or immunocompromise when relevant, and choose empiric therapy from the syndrome, prior microbiology, recent antimicrobials and local resistance rather than one universal regimen.
recognize: Fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain and focal chest findings may occur, but older adults can present with delirium or functional decline.
Hypoxemia, hypotension, altered mental status and rising respiratory effort increase severity regardless of the acquisition label.
differentiate: Viral infection, COPD/asthma exacerbation, heart failure, PE and aspiration pneumonitis can mimic pneumonia.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia is not simply 'more severe CAP'; timing, resistant-organism risk and recent microbiology change empiric choices.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, hemodynamics, mental status, aspiration risk, recent hospitalization/antibiotics, prior resistant organisms, immune status and goals of care.
workup: Use chest imaging when pneumonia is clinically suspected and the result will change management; obtain cultures for severe disease or resistant-organism risk rather than every mild outpatient case.
management: Treat CAP with evidence-based Canadian/local regimens matched to severity and comorbidity; use hospital/local antibiogram pathways for HAP.
Reassess early for treatment failure and source complications such as empyema or obstruction.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum or prolonged therapy; renal/hepatic function and QT/interactions can materially change antibiotic choice.
Do not treat aspiration pneumonitis automatically with antibiotics unless bacterial infection is clinically supported.
counselling: Teach return precautions for worsening dyspnea, confusion, chest pain, inability to hydrate or persistent fever.
followUp: Confirm clinical recovery and review culture/imaging results that require a treatment change or further evaluation.
examTrap: Using a routine outpatient CAP regimen for a deteriorating recently hospitalized patient with resistant-organism risk—or broadening antibiotics for aspiration pneumonitis without bacterial evidence.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia treatment follows severity, setting, microbiology risk and source—not the word pneumonia alone.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory antimicrobial stewardship resources

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Diagnose by Pretest Probability, Then Risk-Stratify the Confirmed PE
bottomLine: Suspected PE uses pretest probability before D-dimer or imaging. Once PE is confirmed, hemodynamic status, right-ventricular strain, biomarkers, bleeding risk and social/clinical suitability determine outpatient anticoagulation versus monitored admission or reperfusion escalation.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain, syncope, hemoptysis, tachycardia and hypoxemia are nonspecific but important in the right risk context.
High-risk PE is defined by hemodynamic instability, not clot size alone.
differentiate: Low pretest probability plus validated rule-out criteria can avoid unnecessary D-dimer/CTPA.
Intermediate-risk PE is not an automatic thrombolysis indication; most stable patients receive anticoagulation with close monitoring.
assessment: Assess pretest probability, bleeding risk, hemodynamics, oxygen need, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, cancer and ability to manage therapy/follow-up safely.
workup: Use validated pretest-probability pathways, sensitive D-dimer when appropriate, and CTPA/VQ imaging according to probability and contraindications.
After confirmation, evaluate RV strain and prognostic markers when they affect disposition/escalation.
management: Start anticoagulation promptly when indicated and safe; eligible low-risk patients may be managed outpatient with reliable follow-up.
High-risk PE requires immediate expert assessment for reperfusion plus anticoagulation; intermediate-high risk requires close monitoring for deterioration.
medicationSafety: DOAC selection depends on renal/hepatic function, pregnancy, cancer context, interactions and bleeding risk.
Do not delay anticoagulation in a high-probability patient solely because imaging is delayed when bleeding risk is acceptable and current guidance supports empiric treatment.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions, recurrence symptoms and when to seek emergency care.
followUp: Ensure rapid outpatient follow-up, duration-of-anticoagulation review and reassessment of provoking factors.
examTrap: Ordering CTPA before estimating pretest probability—or treating every normotensive PE with thrombolysis because the clot burden looks large.
oneLinePearl: PE has two separate decisions: probability before diagnosis, prognosis after diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Pulmonary Embolism Diagnosis, Treatment, and High-/Intermediate-Risk Clinical Guides

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose the Sleep Disorder, Then Treat the Consequence
bottomLine: OSA is diagnosed with sleep testing in a patient whose symptoms/risk justify it; questionnaires estimate risk but do not make the diagnosis. Treatment is matched to severity, symptoms, cardiometabolic risk and anatomy, with CPAP adherence and efficacy assessed rather than simply prescribing a machine.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, nocturnal choking, nonrestorative sleep, morning headache and daytime sleepiness are common clues.
OSA can worsen hypertension, atrial fibrillation, metabolic disease and driving risk.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, sedatives, depression, restless legs and central sleep apnea can mimic sleepiness.
Obesity increases risk but OSA also occurs in non-obese patients with craniofacial/anatomic risk.
assessment: Assess sleepiness, driving/work safety, snoring/apneas, BMI/neck/anatomy, alcohol/sedatives, resistant hypertension, AF and heart failure.
workup: Use validated home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography according to pretest probability, comorbidities and local sleep-medicine pathway.
Do not use an overnight oximetry result alone as a universal OSA diagnosis.
management: Use CPAP for appropriate patients and address weight, alcohol/sedative exposure, positional factors and nasal obstruction.
Consider oral appliance or specialty/anatomic options when appropriate and CPAP is unsuitable.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/opioids can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and driving risk.
Do not prescribe wake-promoting medication as a substitute for treating untreated OSA and inadequate sleep.
redFlags: Dangerous daytime sleepiness while driving/operating machinery
Heart failure or neuromuscular disease complicating sleep-disordered breathing
counselling: Teach mask/interface care, adherence troubleshooting and driving precautions when excessive sleepiness is present.
followUp: Review objective CPAP use/effectiveness, residual symptoms and treatment barriers rather than assuming prescription equals treatment.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from STOP-BANG alone or prescribing CPAP without confirming the sleep-disordered-breathing diagnosis/pathway.
oneLinePearl: Risk tools find who needs sleep testing; they do not replace the sleep study diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian Sleep Society sleep-disordered-breathing resources

title: Pleural Effusion: Transudate, Exudate, Infection, or Malignancy?
bottomLine: Pleural effusion is a sign, not a diagnosis. Determine whether the presentation fits a known transudative process or needs diagnostic sampling, then use fluid chemistry, cell count, microbiology/cytology and imaging to identify infection, malignancy, thrombosis or other exudative disease.
recognize: Dyspnea, pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds/dullness can occur; small effusions may be incidental.
Unilateral, large, recurrent, febrile or unexplained effusions deserve more diagnostic attention than typical bilateral heart-failure effusions.
differentiate: Heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic states commonly cause transudates; pneumonia, malignancy, PE and inflammatory disease commonly cause exudates.
Empyema/complicated parapneumonic effusion requires drainage/source control, not antibiotics alone.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, fever, cancer/VTE risk, heart/renal/liver disease, weight loss, chest pain, anticoagulation and prior imaging.
workup: Use ultrasound/CT when indicated and diagnostic thoracentesis for unexplained or concerning effusions.
Interpret pleural protein/LDH with paired serum studies and add pH/glucose, culture or cytology based on the differential.
management: Treat the cause; drain symptomatic or infected effusions according to severity and procedural pathway.
Refer recurrent malignant/uncertain effusions for definitive pleural management rather than serial taps alone.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric diuretic escalation for a unilateral unexplained effusion without reassessing the diagnosis.
Anticoagulation around pleural procedures is agent- and risk-specific.
redFlags: Recurrent unilateral effusion with malignancy concern
counselling: Explain that fluid testing is intended to find the cause and that the follow-up plan depends on the mechanism.
followUp: Track cytology/culture/imaging results to diagnostic closure and confirm response of the underlying disease.
examTrap: Calling every pleural effusion heart failure and giving more diuretic despite unilateral recurrence, fever or weight loss.
oneLinePearl: Pleural fluid should answer the mechanism: pressure problem, inflammation/infection, clot, or malignancy.
sourceBasis: Canadian pleural-procedure and respirology practice principles

title: Hemoptysis: Stabilize the Airway, Then Find the Bleeding Source
bottomLine: Hemoptysis severity is defined by airway/hemodynamic threat more than an exact millilitre count. First distinguish true lower-airway bleeding from nasopharyngeal or GI blood, stabilize significant bleeding, then evaluate infection, malignancy, bronchiectasis, PE and vascular causes.
recognize: Bright-red blood with cough suggests respiratory source, but swallowed epistaxis and hematemesis can mimic it.
Cancer risk, bronchiectasis, TB exposure, anticoagulation and PE symptoms change urgency and differential.
differentiate: Blood-streaked sputum in a stable URI is different from ongoing bleeding with hypoxemia or airway compromise.
Normal chest x-ray does not end the workup when recurrent hemoptysis or malignancy risk remains significant.
assessment: Assess airway, oxygenation, hemodynamics, estimated bleeding trajectory, anticoagulants, infection/TB risk, smoking/cancer risk and PE symptoms.
workup: Use CBC/coagulation/renal studies as relevant and chest imaging based on severity/risk; CT/bronchoscopy may be required for recurrent or high-risk bleeding.
management: Significant ongoing bleeding requires emergency airway/respirology/interventional management and positioning/airway strategy according to source and local protocol.
Treat the underlying infection, tumor, bronchiectasis or thrombosis once stabilized.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant reversal decisions depend on severity, agent and thrombosis risk and require current protocol.
Avoid NSAIDs/antiplatelet escalation while clinically important active bleeding is unexplained.
counselling: Teach that recurrent hemoptysis requires evaluation even if each episode is small.
followUp: Ensure imaging/bronchoscopy/cancer or infection follow-up is completed after stabilization.
examTrap: Reassuring recurrent hemoptysis because the chest x-ray is normal or because the estimated volume is below a memorized cutoff.
oneLinePearl: In hemoptysis, airway threat and bleeding trajectory matter more than a single volume estimate.
sourceBasis: Canadian respiratory and acute-care hemoptysis practice principles

title: Chronic Cough: Confirm Duration, Find the Common Causes, Respect the Red Flags
bottomLine: Chronic cough needs a structured cause-based workup, not repeated empiric antibiotic courses. Confirm duration and medication/exposure history, look for upper-airway disease, asthma/eosinophilic disease, reflux and smoking-related disease, and escalate hemoptysis, weight loss, hypoxemia or abnormal imaging.
recognize: ACE inhibitors, smoking/vaping, rhinitis/postnasal symptoms, asthma, reflux and chronic airway disease are common contributors.
More than one cause can coexist, so partial response to one treatment does not end the evaluation.
differentiate: Persistent cough after infection can last weeks but should trend toward recovery; recurrent fever, hemoptysis or progressive dyspnea needs another diagnosis.
GERD treatment should not be reflexively prescribed to every cough without reflux features or a defensible trial rationale.
assessment: Ask duration, triggers, sputum, hemoptysis, dyspnea, reflux/nasal symptoms, medication list, smoking/vaping/cannabis, occupational exposure and cancer/TB risk.
workup: Use chest x-ray and spirometry when indicated by chronicity/risk; add bronchoprovocation, CT, ENT or GI evaluation only when the history/initial workup supports it.
management: Remove causative medication/exposure when appropriate and treat the most likely cause with a defined reassessment interval.
Refer unexplained refractory cough after structured evaluation rather than stacking indefinite empiric therapies.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotics when bacterial infection is unsupported.
Opioid antitussives and sedating cough products can cause harm and should not substitute for diagnosis.
counselling: Explain the stepwise diagnostic plan and that chronic cough often has more than one contributor.
followUp: Reassess after each targeted intervention and document whether the cough actually changed before adding another therapy.
examTrap: Giving a fourth antibiotic course for chronic cough without checking ACE inhibitor use, smoking, spirometry or chest imaging indications.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough is solved by a structured differential and response-to-treatment loop, not serial empiricism.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society cough resources and Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory principles
